extracted.intended_audience: orators, writers, and students of rhetoric/classical literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on producing 'the Sublime' in literature and oratory: principles of diction, figures (metaphor, periphrasis, hyperbole), arrangement (harmony, rhythm, period), and the balance of genius and art. Applicable to prose and poetic composition aiming for elevated effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periphrasis (circumlocution) tends to sublimity
rubrics_metrics.description: None, I suppose, would dispute the fact that periphrasis tends much to sublimity. For, as in music the simple air is rendered more pleasing by the addition of harmony, so in language periphrasis often sounds in concord with a literal expression, adding much to the beauty of its tone,--provided always that it is not inflated and harsh, but agreeably blended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use periphrasis to harmonise and dignify simple ideas (example: calling Death the 'destined journey'). Do not let it become inflated or harsh; it must be agreeably blended with literal expression. Abuse leads to feebleness and disgust (see Plato's criticized uses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of appropriate and striking words
rubrics_metrics.description: The choice of appropriate and striking words has a marvellous power and an enthralling charm for the reader ... beautiful words are the very light of thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritise striking, appropriate diction: the right words enliven thought and bestow grandeur. However, adapt register to occasion—imposing language is not appropriate to every subject (using high diction for trivial subject is absurd).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of register to occasion
rubrics_metrics.description: I do not mean to say that imposing language is appropriate to every occasion. A trifling subject tricked out in grand and stately words would have the same effect as a huge tragic mask placed on the head of a little child.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match diction and rhetorical ornament to the subject's gravity. Avoid grandiose language for trivial topics; this incongruity weakens effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of plain/homely language for vividness
rubrics_metrics.description: The most homely language is sometimes far more vivid than the most ornamental, being recognised at once as the language of common life, and gaining immediate currency by its familiarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not disdain simple, colloquial expressions when they give greater vividness or immediacy (examples: Theophrastus' 'taking doses of trouble', Herodotus' brutal plainness). Plainness can be more expressive than ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metaphor: potency and risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Metaphors conduce to sublimity ... these, and a hundred similar fancies ... are sufficient to demonstrate how great is the natural power of figurative language, and how largely metaphors conduce to sublimity ... That the use of figurative language, as of all other beauties of style, has a constant tendency towards excess, is an obvious truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use metaphors to elevate thought and produce vivid imagery. Be aware metaphors readily lead to excess; exercise restraint and judgment to avoid inflated or violent allegory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of metaphors in one place should be limited (usually 2–3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concerning the number of metaphors to be employed together Caecilius seems to give his vote with those critics who make a law that not more than two, or at the utmost three, should be combined in the same place. The use, however, must be determined by the occasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a rule, avoid clustering more than two or three metaphors in the same locus; nevertheless, allow exceptions when the occasion (e.g., violent passion or torrent-like outburst) calls for many metaphors to convey force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passion/feeling justifies audacious or many metaphors
rubrics_metrics.description: Those outbursts of passion which drive onwards like a winter torrent draw with them as an indispensable accessory whole masses of metaphor ... they absolutely demand as indispensable the use of daring metaphors, and will not allow the hearer to pause and criticise the number of them, because he shares the passion of the speaker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When genuine, intense feeling animates discourse, more and bolder metaphors become credible and effective—the audience shares the passion and forgives otherwise excessive ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soften harsh metaphors by hedging phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle and Theophrastus recommend the softening of harsh metaphors by the use of some such phrase as 'So to say,' 'As it were,' 'If I may be permitted the expression,' 'If so bold a term is allowable.' For thus to forestall criticism mitigates, they assert, the boldness of the metaphors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a metaphor risks criticism or harshness, use parenthetical hedges to pre-empt objections and reduce the perceived boldness of the figure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extended series of metaphors for descriptive distinctness
rubrics_metrics.description: In the treatment, again, of familiar topics and in descriptive passages nothing gives such distinctness as a close and continuous series of metaphors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ a sustained chain of related metaphors in descriptive writing to delineate features vividly and cohesively (Xenophon's anatomical descriptions are cited as examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Restraint: figures easily become excessive
rubrics_metrics.description: But this figure, more than any other, is very liable to abuse, and great restraint is required in employing it. It soon begins to carry an impression of feebleness, savours of vapid trifling, and arouses disgust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuously monitor for overuse: when figures become routine or forced they appear weak and trivial. Prune excess; prefer natural, earned figurative use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyperbole: credible when natural or disguised; avoid absurd overstrain
rubrics_metrics.description: The hyperbole is then most effective when it appears in disguise ... This effect is produced when a writer, impelled by strong feeling, speaks in the accents of some tremendous crisis ... We can see that these circumstances have not been dragged in to produce a hyperbole, but that the hyperbole has grown naturally out of the circumstances. Such absurdities as, 'Unless you carry your brains next to the ground in your heels.' Hence it is necessary to know where to draw the line; for if ever it is overstepped the effect of the hyperbole is spoilt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let exaggeration arise organically from the depicted situation (e.g., scenes of frenzy), and conceal obvious rhetorical stretching. Avoid fanciful, unbelievable hyperboles that break credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmony and arrangement of words (composition akin to music)
rubrics_metrics.description: Harmony is an instrument which has a natural power, not only to win and to delight, but also in a remarkable degree to exalt the soul and sway the heart of man ... composition (being a kind of harmony of that language which nature has taught us) ... by the blending of its manifold tones it brings home to the minds of those who stand by the feelings present to the speaker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shape sentences with attention to cadence, modulation, and the ordering of words: reserve key phrases for later position, use measures and pauses to produce solemnity, and aim for a 'musical' unison between form and idea (Demosthenes' dactylic cadence is an example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Periodic construction: rounding the period increases power
rubrics_metrics.description: As the different members of the body ... unite by their mutual combination to form a complete and perfect organism, so also the elements of a fine passage ... when joined in one organic whole, and still further compacted by the bond of harmony, by the mere rounding of the period gain power of tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct sentences so their parts accumulate and culminate—an organic, rounded period gives dignity and gravitas. Avoid disjointed or hasty constructions that dissipate force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-rhythmical, effeminate, or monotonous cadence
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing so much degrades the tone of a style as an effeminate and hurried movement in the language, such as is produced by pyrrhics and trochees ... Such abuse of rhythm is sure to savour of coxcombry and petty affectation, and grows tiresome ... an over-rhythmical passage does not affect the hearer by the meaning of its words, but merely by their cadence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let regular, dance-like rhythms dominate prose—if listeners anticipate pauses or 'beat time' with the cadence, the meaning is lost. Vary rhythm to keep emphasis on sense rather than tune.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid cramping (over-compression) and over-extension of diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Sublimity is further diminished by cramping the diction. Deformity instead of grandeur ensues from over-compression. ... On the other hand, we know that a style becomes lifeless by over-extension, I mean by being relaxed to an unseasonable length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strike a balance: be concise where directness is called for, but avoid cutting words so short that sense is pruned away; likewise avoid undue prolixity that relaxes force. Aim for proportionate compression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction: avoid mean, petty, or vulgar words in grand passages
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of mean words has also a strong tendency to degrade a lofty passage ... 'wore away' is ignoble and vulgar, and 'unwelcome' inadequate to the extent of the disaster.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select elevated, fitting vocabulary for sublime subjects; petty or colloquial terms can mar an otherwise magnificent passage. Replace low-sounding terms with broader, more dignified phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid incongruous petty details in grand description (use broad strokes)
rubrics_metrics.description: He runs off from the grander parts of his subject to the meaner, and sinks where he ought to rise ... by his mixing up panniers and spices and bags with his wonderful recital of that vast and busy scene one would imagine that he was describing a kitchen ... These petty words, introduced out of season, stand out like deformities and blots on the diction. These details might have been given in one or two broad strokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing magnificence, avoid enumerating trivial, incongruous minutiae that collapse the grandeur; prefer aggregated, broad descriptions or grouped categories to preserve majesty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genius (loftiness) overruns pedantic correctness—prefer grandeur with faults
rubrics_metrics.description: Is it not worth while to raise the whole question whether in poetry and prose we should prefer sublimity accompanied by some faults, or a style which never rising above moderate excellence never stumbles and never requires correction?... I still think that the greater excellences, though not everywhere equally sustained, ought always to be voted to the first place in literature ... the loftier walks of literature are by their very loftiness perilous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value striking, lofty originality even when it brings occasional lapses; sublime genius that risks faults often produces work of higher lasting value than faultless mediocrity. Use art to temper nature, but do not subordinate greatness to mere correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art should assist nature; combine technical skill with natural genius
rubrics_metrics.description: Since that success which consists in avoidance of error is usually the gift of art, while high, though unequal excellence is the attribute of genius, it is proper on all occasions to call in art as an ally to nature. By the combined resources of these two we may hope to achieve perfection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate craft (attention to detail, stylistic rules, and correction) to support raw creative power; combine technique and innate loftiness for best results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mixing grand thought with ignoble phrasing—maintain dignity of utterance
rubrics_metrics.description: In our sublimer efforts we should never stoop to what is sordid and despicable, unless very hard pressed by some urgent necessity. If we would write becomingly, our utterance should be worthy of our theme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve a tone commensurate with the theme; only when context demands should one intentionally descend to sordid or low diction, and then with purpose.
